Noah acked and pulled canary logs plus baseline store status.
Grafana showed the paging rule's firing alerts increasing.
Allison asked whether only paging rules or warnings too were firing, and whether paging was just flipped on in more dimensions.
Rafael said paging rules were the issue; warning rules were also firing.

Sofia found queueing time roughly flat on a 'regressed' model, but queries showed many new label combinations.
Logan suspected a cardinality change linked to that week's schema review.

Vanessa offered to check last-hour fleet changes but noted cross-region simultaneity pointed to config/telemetry.
Rafael set the immediate goal of stopping paging noise, proposing disabling paging rules or canary evaluation during triage.

Runbook option 2: disable paging rules in observability-pack.
Runbook option 3: lower canary QPS to near-zero.

Distribution drift in prompt_bucket creates new series without baselines, so the evaluator may fall back to a poor default.

If canary emits extra labels not stripped before lookup, baseline is 'not found' and evaluator may treat baseline as 0 or default.
links.conditions: extra labels emitted and not stripped in lookup

links.description: Evaluator keys baseline fetch on the full labelset unless baseline_key_labels is set; it was unset in prod.

links.description: Allison characterized the incident as a config regression and asked why it surfaced now.
A runtime PR added the kernel_id tag to telemetry.
The canary began emitting kernel_id in us-east the day before the incident.
Enabling paging rules for 'top models' on the incident day, combined with new labels, made the storm blow up.
Caleb noted telemetry ingestion delay during the incident; recorded later as a contributing cause.
Ingestion lag can distort minimum-samples logic.
